title: Winding the strap (Hosea 2:21–22)
hook: wrapping the finger, many say "And I will betroth thee unto Me for ever"

segments.voice: Yesterday, the head box, above the hairline, and God's own tefillin. Your line was thoughts get bound too. Did your fingers find your forehead? Today, the last step of putting them on. Day one hundred forty-two.

A wedding ring is a small thing. A thin band of metal. Yet some people touch theirs all day without noticing, turn it when they're nervous, miss it for weeks if they take it off. It's not what it's made of. It's what it says: I'm bound to someone, and they're bound to me. Now, the last moment of putting on tefillin. Both boxes are on. The long strap from the arm is still hanging free. The person takes it and, slowly, wraps it around one finger. Three times. Like a ring.
screen: `A THIN BAND OF METAL.` → `WHAT IT SAYS: BOUND.` → `THREE TIMES AROUND ONE FINGER.`

segments.voice: After the head box is on, the rest of the arm strap is wound around the hand. It's wrapped three times around the middle finger, and then across the palm, often in a way that traces the shape of the letter shin, for Shaddai, the name we met yesterday. The customs differ: Ashkenazi, Sephardi and Hasidic Jews wind in different directions and patterns, and each is handed down from parents and teachers. As they wrap the finger, many say two verses from the prophet Hosea. In Hosea, God speaks to the people like a spouse after a long, painful separation, promising to start again: "And I will betroth thee unto Me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto Me in righteousness, and in justice, and in lovingkindness, and in compassion. And I will betroth thee unto Me in faithfulness; and thou shalt know the LORD." Betroth. That's engagement language. From the same Hebrew root comes erusin, the first stage of a Jewish marriage. So the last act of putting on tefillin is a kind of daily wedding: the strap around the finger like a ring, and the words of a promise. Notice what's promised: righteousness, justice, lovingkindness, compassion, faithfulness. It's not a list of feelings. It's a list of how two parties treat each other. And notice: Hosea's words come after a story of betrayal and hurt. The promise isn't made by people who've never failed each other. It's made by people starting again. Every weekday morning, before the main prayers, the people who say these verses renew it.
screen: `THREE TIMES AROUND THE FINGER.` · `CUSTOMS DIFFER, HANDED DOWN.` · `I WILL BETROTH THEE UNTO ME.` · `A PROMISE MADE AFTER A BREAK.` · then, large: `LIKE A RING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wear a ring or bracelet mindfully. If you're wearing one now, touch it. If not, wrap a finger of one hand in the other. Settle, and breathe. Think of one relationship you're committed to: a partner, a friend, a parent, a child, or, if you pray, God. Which of Hosea's five would you want to bring to it today? Righteousness, justice, kindness, compassion, faithfulness. Choose one. Hold the ring while you choose. The bell holds the time.
Winding the strap. The last step of putting on tefillin: three turns around the finger, like a ring, with Hosea's words of betrothal.
Your line: like a ring. Every time you touch a ring, a bracelet or your own hand today, remember the one quality you chose. Day one hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: After the head box, the arm strap is wound around the middle finger and hand; many Jews say Hosea 2:21–22 as they wrap the finger three times. Winding customs differ between Ashkenazi, Sephardi and Hasidic communities.

what it means: a daily ring and a daily promise, made in Hosea's words.
what a scholar hears: Hosea 2:21–22 (2:19–20 in Christian Bibles) closes a chapter about a broken marriage; erusin is the legal first stage of Jewish marriage; winding customs vary by community.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Hosea 2:21–22 (the JPS lays it out as poetry with 'Yea' and 'And' capitalized at line starts; normalized here to prose capitalization). Keeper/editor to confirm.
Hosea 2:21–22 in Hebrew numbering = 2:19–20 in Christian Bibles.
Saying Hosea while winding is a widespread custom (Ashkenazi and others), not law. Confirm.
Shin traced on the hand: Ashkenazi custom; Sephardi and Hasidic patterns differ. Confirm phrasing.
Hebrew in the original game: וְאֵרַשְׂתִּיךְ לִי לְעוֹלָם — confirm vocalization.

Editor review (Oct 2026): SERIOUS fix: the teach said 'three verses' from Hosea; the quoted passage is two verses (Hosea 2:21–22). Also: hook no longer opens 'Think about' / 'Now picture'; 'people... feel strange' softened to 'some people'; erusin tied to the verse's root rather than called 'the Hebrew word'; 'before a word of the main prayers' softened.
